Workshop requirements¶

There are 2 ways to carry on with the workshop:

  1. Using Anaconda (on your computer, install required). This is the preferred way.
    We will use Spyder (desktop, most advanced) and JupyterLab (notebooks, most user friendly)
  2. Using a Binder (online). If you don't want to install python on your computer but still want to run the python examples.
    You can run and modify code during the workshop, but changes are not saved. The Binder is that same as the Workshop notebook but you can run the code within.

If option 1: Install/Download BEFORE the workshop (you probably already did this)¶

Do the following BEFORE the beginning of the workshop (ideally the day before). This takes about 40 minutes, at reasonably good internet speed.

  1. Install Anaconda, which is a free "bundle" of Python and many modules, libraries and other programs commonly used in scientific research. Please install Anaconda from here: https://www.anaconda.com/download. Install is free, but you need to create an account for the download.

  2. Once Anaconda finishes installing, open the Anaconda Navigator. Sometimes this is automatically opened after the installation finishes. If not, search in the Windows Taskbar (in Mac, search in the Launchpad) for "Anaconda Navigator".

  1. Once Anaconda Navigator is open, take a look at the available applications, find the application named “Spyder” (option 1a) and “JupyterLab”. If it is already installed, there will be a “Launch” button… if it is NOT installed, there will be a “Install” button. Make sure Spyder and JupyterLab are installed (by clicking on the ”Install” button)… but you may NOT want to “launch” it just yet. Wait until you finish installing the packages shown below.
  2. Open the Anaconda Prompt (Windows) or Terminal (Mac). Easiest way is by searching in the Windows Taskbar the term "Anaconda Prompt" (Windows) or search in the Launchpad for "Terminal" (Mac). Then follow the next steps to install 3 modules (i.e. netcdf4, cartopy and cmocean):
  • Install netcdf4, by copy-pasting in the Anaconda Prompt (or Terminal):
conda install -c anaconda netcdf4

  • Click [Enter]

  • If it asks you "are you sure?", type "y" and click [Enter] again.

  • Install cartopy, by copy-pasting in the Anaconda Prompt (or Terminal):

conda install -c conda-forge cartopy

  • Click [Enter]

  • If it asks you "are you sure?", type "y" and click [Enter] again.

  • Install cmocean, by copy-pasting in the Anaconda Prompt (or Terminal):

conda install -c conda-forge cmocean
  • Click [Enter]
  • If it asks you "are you sure?", type "y" and click [Enter] again.

  1. Do this step only the day prior to the workshop, otherwise the link will not work. Get the workshop files from GitHub. Download the workshop repository from here: https://github.com/alaurent101/WYTEC2_Python_Workshop/archive/refs/heads/main.zip

    By default the file downloaded with be named WYTEC2_Python_Workshop-main.zip. Unzip the file anywhere on your computer. By default the folder will be named WYTEC2_Python_Workshop-main but make sure you rename it to WYTEC2_Python_Workshop because we will use this name during the tutorial. The folder WYTEC2_Python_Workshop will be the working directory for the workshop.

  2. On the day of the workshop you just have to open Anaconda and know the path to the workshop folder.

If Option 2: You don't have to install anything before the workshop¶

  1. On the day of the workshop, load the binder in your web browser

The Binder will be available here: https://mybinder.org/v2/gh/alaurent101/WYTEC2_Python_Workshop/HEAD?urlpath=%2Fdoc%2Ftree%2FWYTEC2_PythonTutorial.ipynb

It should take a couple of minutes to load the tutorial and you'll be ready to go.

Workshop mechanics (how to work through the workshop)¶

If running python locally with Anaconda (option 1)¶

For this workshop you will need 3 programs (sometimes 4):

  1. Workshop notebook: It is this web-page, which has the instructions on what to do in the lab. The webpage will be available on the day of the tutorial (and after).
  2. Spyder: This is the desktop program that you will use to write and run Python code. We'll talk more about Spyder.
  3. JupyterLab: This is the notebook program that you will also use to write and run Python code. We'll talk more about JupyterLab.
  4. Terminal: Every once in a while you will need to install additional Python modules. This is done in the Terminal. More on this during the workshop.

In the first part of the workshop, you will be required to read along the Workshop notebook and copy-paste code from the Workshop notebook into Spyder to run it. This will create output in the form of numbers, graphs, maps, etc. So you will be jumping back and forth between the Workshop notebook and Spyder throughout the first part of the Workshop.
In the second part of the workshop, we will work directly on the Workshop notebook with JupyterLab.

If using the binder (option 2)¶

You just need to follow along the tutorial. Instead of going to Spyder, as explained above, during the first part of the tutorial, you can run the commands directly in the Binder.
The second part of the tutorial will look the same as in Anaconda because it uses JupyterLab.

Where is my code?¶

Data, code and the results produced by the code can be stored in many places, including "the cloud" (e.g. Google-Drive, GitHub, a website, etc.) and physical computers including the computer that you are working on at this moment. Additionally, within your computer, data and code can be stored in the hard-drive, in memory and on the screen.

Note that:

  • Computers can ONLY see and work with code and data stored in memory
  • Humans can ONLY see code and data shown on the screen
  • When turning your computer off, code/data in both the memory and the screen are lost forever! Therefore, make sure that you save your work on your hard-drive or the cloud, before turning your computer off.

We will see below how to move code (and data) between all these storage areas (i.e. memory, hard-drive, screen, cloud). keeping track of where is your code/data stored, is one of the most common sources of errors during coding.

Anaconda (downloading and installing Python)¶

There are many ways to install Python. Here, we'll used one of the most common methods... we installed Anaconda (likely you already did this earlier, in preparation for this workshop!). Anaconda is a free "bundle" of Python and many modules, libraries and other programs commonly used in scientific research. If you haven't done so, please install Anaconda from here: https://www.anaconda.com/download. You just need to create an account to download.

Note that when you installed Anaconda, a lot of code was copied from "The Cloud" into your hard-drive, in a location that we will call "the Python Directory". The actual location of "the Python Directory" is not important to us in this workshop. However if you are curious and try to find it, just make sure that you DO NOT move, delete or add anything within "the Python Directory"! You can break Python's proper functioning.

Spyder¶

Most people do "coding" (in any programming language) using an "Integrated Development Environment" (IDE), which are programs designed to make "coding" easier. IDE's make it easier to run your code, get help, manage multiple projects and files, color-code your code as you write it, etc. IDE's are like a Swiss-army-knife for coding. Many IDE's are free. Take a look at this list of IDE's

In the first part of this lab, we'll use Spyder, which is a free "Integrated Development Environment" that comes included in Anaconda and that is especially designed to work with Python. You should already have it installed in your computer if you downloaded Anaconda.

JupyterLab¶

Another way to do programming with an interface is to use "Notebooks" that include live code, visualizations, text and equations. For Python Jupyter Notebook is a popular, open-source web-based interactive computational environment (it also supports other languages like Julia or R). This tutorial was created with a Jupyter Notebook. JupyterLab is the next-generation user interface for Notebooks that provides an IDE-like experience. We will use JupyterLab in the second part of the workshop.

Part 1 - Python basics with Spyder¶

  • To open Spyder, search in the taskbar for "Spyder" or click on its icon in the Anaconda-Navigator, the program looks as follows:

Note that when you open Spyder, behind the scenes a bunch of code was loaded into memory from "the Python Directory" (i.e. hard-drive).

Spyder's overview¶

The Spyder screen is divided in multiple panels. The two most important are the Console and the Editor.

Spyder's "Console"¶

The Console (also known as the interpreter) is a live instance of Python. This is the place where Python will display error messages, warnings, and some code output. The Console is also where you can quickly interact with Python by writing code and then clicking [Enter] (note that when you click [Enter], anything you wrote on the Console will be loaded to memory and executed immediately).

Note that, to help you figure out what to type in the "Console" and what to type (or copy-paste) in the "Editor", we added a small colored box with instructions above every "code box" (red to type in "Console" and green to type in "Editor").

Let's try it:


In [ ]:
print('hello world!')

hello world!

After you typed in the console print('hello world!')... and clicked [Enter]...

What got displayed on the screen?



Spyder's "Working Directory"¶

The working directory is the location in your computer hard-drive where Spyder is reading and writing files. In the top right corner (usually), Spyder will show you its working directory.

To change the working directory, simply chick on the "folder" icon and select the new location. When you execute Python code with instructions to write data or a figure to a file, this file will be save by default in the working directory.


  1. Earlier, in the setup/downloads/installs BEFORE the workshop, you should have downloaded the workshop repository from GitHub and unzipped it on your computer. By default the zip file is named WYTEC2_Python_Workshop-main.zip and when you unzip it it creates the folder WYTEC2_Python_Workshop-main. Make sure you rename this folder WYTEC2_Python_Workshop because we will use this name in the tutorial. Now your folder WYTEC2_Python_Workshop should contain the subfolder binder, css, data,images and scripts plus 6 files. Those are all you need for the tutorial. Make sure it looks similar to the screenshot below. If not you might not be in the right directory.

  2. Change Spyder's working directory to point to your WYTEC2_Python_Workshop folder.


Note: In the "script" above (Python file) the path to the data file starts with ./. That means Python will assume that the path starts in the current directory. If the folder data is not there it will fail. You could also have your data folder somewhere else on your computer but you need to provide the full path, for example like in the example above it could be: C:\Users\MyName\Work\data\buoy_data.csv



Take a look at Spyder's working directory (top-right corner) to verify that indeed Spyder is pointing to the correct location.

You can also see the location of the working directory by typing the following in the console (then press [Enter]):


In [ ]:
%pwd

Spyder's "Editor"¶

The Editor is the space where you write your code so that you can execute it later. The Editor is shown below inside the green box.

The Editor is just a text editor like Notepad (in Windows) or TextEdit (in Mac). However, Spyder's Editor color-codes your text so that it can be read with ease. It will also perform some basic quality control and will tell you if you made a mistake (more on this later).

You can run the code you wrote in the editor by clicking on the "run" button (i.e. green triangular button shown below).

Note that the first time you run your code the Editor will prompt you to save your file. You can name your file anything you want, but the extension will be automatically set as .py, which is the default extension for Python files. Also note that, by default, you will be prompt to save your file in the current working directory. Make sure the file is saved in the workshop directory otherwise Python will not find the data files to run the Real-Life examples.

After you write some code in the Editor, note that clicking the "save" button technically transfers code from the Screen into a file in your hard-drive. Also, if you click the "run" button, it automatically saves your code and then loads it into memory and executes it!

In Spyder, you can click on [File] > [New file...] to create a new empty Python file.

Make a new file, name it test1.py, and save it in your working directory.

Note that, to help you figure out when to type or copy-paste into the "Editor" (i.e. NOT in the "Console"), we added a small GREEN colored box with instructions above every "code box".

Lets do a test. Type the following in the Editor and click

In [2]:
print('hello world!')

hello world!

As you see, when you run the code in the Editor, the output is displayed in the Console

a) Code is saved to the hard-drive

c) Code is saved to the cloud

d) Code is loaded to the screen

When to "Editor"? ...and when to "Console"?¶

It can be tricky to know when to type (or copy-paste) code in the "Editor" and when to do so in the "Console". The "Editor" is best suited for writing long (or medium length) scripts that are self-contained... while the "Console" is best for writing "on the fly" tests that are one or a few lines long.

  1. Editor: When you use Editor you most save your code in a .py file before you can it. The advantage of this is that you can re-use your code at a later date. Simply open your .py file and it again! Use the Editor to write self-contained code (i.e. scripts or little programs) that you may want to re-use a later date. Examples of these self-contained scripts are shown in the real-life case studies below.

  2. Console: The Console is the quickest way to enter code into Python's "memory" and the quickest way to query or inspect something that is already in Python's "memory". The drawback is that code written in Console quickly disappears as you write new code... or when you turn off Spyder or your computer. Code written in the Console is not very re-usable. Therefore, use the Console when you need to do "one-offs" or "on the fly" tests.



If we use, as an analogy, the development of a new recipe for making "chicken tacos". You may start cooking the recipe as you write each step in your recipe book. When you get to the part about adding salt, you don't know how much salt to add... so you experiment. You start by adding a small amount of salt (1 gr), stir and taste. If it is not enough, you ad another gram... then stir and taste... and so, on until you get the right amount of salt. Then you write in your recipe the final amount of grams of salt.

In this analogy, writing in the recipe book is as writing in Spyder's "Editor". Text here are clean instructions that you will need to read later to cook the recipe, so these instructions better be clean, well written, and in the appropriate order.

Adding salt, stirring and tasting are "on the fly" tests to see if what you are doing is good or needs adjustment. This is the equivalent to writing in Spyder's "Console".

As mentioned earlier, we will be adding "red" or "green" blocks (like the ones below) to guide you when to use the Console and when to use the Editor...


Comments and statements¶

  • Comments are lines of text meant to be read ONLY by humans (i.e. the computer ignores these lines). Comments usually contain annotations and additional information to make easier to understand the code to the programmer. Comments are preceded by a # (hashtag)

  • A Statement is a line of text read by the computer. This is "the code". A statement contains instructions for the computer to do one or more tasks.

Take a look to the sequence of statements below:

In [5]:
# This is a Comment because it is preceded by a # (hashtag)
a = 2

# Lets print our variables to screen
print(a) # Note that comments can be written after a statement (but not before)

2

Above...

  • The first line is a comment
  • The second line is a statement assigning the value of a to be equal to 2
  • Then there is a blank line. Blank lines are ignored by Python (they exist to space the code and make it easier to read).
  • The forth line is a comment
  • The fifth line is a statement asking Python to print the value of a to screen. After the statement, there is another comment

If you copy-paste the code above to the Spyder's Editor and click [run], it will print a 2 to the console.

Once `a = 2` has been executed, the value of `a` will be stored "in memory" until you turn off python, until you delete `a`, or until you update `a` with a different value.

Variables¶

A Variable is a user-defined label that can be used to name anything. For example, in the statement above (a = 2) "a" is a variable. You can name variables anything you want (no punctuation thought), for example:


In [6]:
my_cute_variable = 35

print(my_cute_variable)

35

Note that it is a good practice to choose variable names that describe what is stored within the variable.

Also note that you can use Spyder's Variable explorer to see what variables are currently loaded into memory.

Sneak-peak of Real-life case study #1: data from an oceanographic buoy outside Halifax Harbour¶

Let's take a quick look at what is coming ahead.

Lets use data from an autonomous buoy located just outside the Halifax Harbour (Canada), which broadcasts real-time weather/ocean data via the following server: https://www.smartatlantic.ca/erddap/tabledap/SMA_halifax.html. Surface temperature data were downloaded in a csv file with this url. The file is named buoy_data.csv and is located in the data folder.


Smartatlantic buoy
Buoy location (Halifax, Canada)

The following code load the buoy's data, and makes a simple plot. Copy/paste the following over the previous code in the Editor and click


In [ ]:
# Import Pandas module
import pandas as pd

# Read data from file
buoy_data = pd.read_csv('./data/buoy_data.csv', skiprows=[1])

# Do quick plot
buoy_data.plot(x='time',y='surface_temp_avg', rot=90)

To see the plot you just made, click on the "Plot" tab (beside your "Variable explorer"). See below...

If you take a close look to the code, you can also see some of the principles that we just learned, like "comments" and "statements":

You can also see in the code that we created a variable (buoy_data) and then we used it to make a plot.

But also there is a lot that we have not learned yet, like modules, fundtions, methods, strings, floats, etc.

We are going to learn those concepts next. Then we'll come back to the Real-life scenario #1: The Oregon Buoy.

Basic data types (or "primitive" data types)¶

In every computer language there are many data types. Each data type is best suited to handle different data, and also behaves under different rules, thus it is important to always be aware of what data type each statement is working with.

Below are some of the most common data types used in Python:

Integers¶

Integers are "round" numbers (i.e. no decimal point).


In [8]:
my_int = 2

print(my_int)

2

Floats¶

Floats are numbers with a decimal point.


In [9]:
my_float = 2.4

print(my_float)

2.4

Strings¶

Strings are letters. Note that you need to wrap the content of the string within quotes to tell Python they are a string.


In [10]:
# You can use single quotes ' or double quotes " to create strings
my_string_1 = 'hello'

my_string_2 = "2.4"

print(my_string_1)
print(my_string_2)

hello
2.4

Note that even though "2.4" is a number, it will be treated by Python as "letters". Therefore you won't be able to do math with "2.4"¶

3

What data type is the following: 324.91


a) Integer

b) Float

c) String

d) Boolean

3

What data type is the following: 'the house is green'


a) Integer

b) Float

c) String

d) Boolean

4

What data type is the following: 87572


a) Integer

b) Float

c) String

d) Boolean

5

If you execute the following line in Python... 

a = 32

Then, what is "32"?

a) an integer

b) a float

c) a string

d) a variable

6

If you execute the following line in Python... 

a = 32

Then, what is "a"?

a) an integer

b) a float

c) a string

d) a variable

Simple operations between different data types¶

You can do math with most of these data types, as long as they are of the same data type. For example:

In [11]:
4 + 7
Out[11]:
11
In [12]:
my_int * 7
Out[12]:
14
In [13]:
my_float / 2
Out[13]:
1.2

Sometimes (not always) you can do math with different data types. However, some quirks and changes may happen to the result. For example, adding an integer plus a float yields a float.

In [14]:
my_int + my_float
Out[14]:
4.4

...but sometimes mixing data types doesn't work. For example, operations between strings and floats (or integers) is not allowed and therefore if you try to do this operation, Python will yield an ERROR.

In [15]:
my_float + my_string_1

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[15], line 1
----> 1 my_float + my_string_1

TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'float' and 'str'

"Summing" two strings simply concatenates them together:

In [16]:
my_string_1 + my_string_2
Out[16]:
'hello2.4'
7

If you execute the following lines in Python...

a = 3
b = 1

Then, what is the result of: a + b

a) 4

b) 3

c) '31'

d) '4'

8

If you execute the following lines in Python...

a = '3'
b = '1'

Then, what is the result of: a + b

a) 4

b) 3

c) '31'

d) '4'

Objects (lists and dictionaries)¶

Everything in Python is an object! Even the basic data types are objects: Integers are "Integer Objects", floats are "Float Objects", etc. Each type of object behaves under its own set of rules, therefore it is ESSENTIAL to be aware of what type of object is each of your variables.

We already talked about the sometimes called "primitive objects" (i.e. integers, floats, strings), however python comes included with some more advanced objects (e.g. lists and dictionaries). Also, when you install new modules, often they come with their own objects (each with their own rules).

Following a "cooking analogy", I like to think "primitive objects" as types of raw ingredients (e.g. liquid, powder, solid) and the more advanced objects can be thought as containers (e.g. bag, basket, jar, shelf).

If you don't know what type of object is a variable, just type type(variableName), for example:

In [17]:
my_var = 12.8

type(my_var)
Out[17]:
float

Lists¶

Lists are similar to "cell-arrays" in Matlab. "Lists" are great when you just want to append items at the end of the list, but you don't care too much about retrieving a particular item within the list.

Let's do a "list"

In [18]:
my_list = [2,5,8,7,1,2,7]

my_list
Out[18]:
[2, 5, 8, 7, 1, 2, 7]

To see if a variable is a list, you can also use type. See below:

In [19]:
type(my_list)
Out[19]:
list

To access an item within the list, type its index within square brackets:

In [20]:
my_list[0]
Out[20]:
2

Note that in Python, the first index is zero!

In [21]:
my_list[1]
Out[21]:
5
In [22]:
my_list[2]
Out[22]:
8

Negative indices are counted backwards from the last item:

In [23]:
my_list[-1]
Out[23]:
7
In [24]:
my_list[-2]
Out[24]:
2

To access several items within the list, use a colon (i.e. :)

In [25]:
my_list[2:4]
Out[25]:
[8, 7]
In [26]:
my_list[:3]
Out[26]:
[2, 5, 8]
In [27]:
my_list[-3:]
Out[27]:
[1, 2, 7]

Note that you can put anything you want in a list (i.e. not only integers). For example:

In [28]:
my_other_list = ['a','5',8,'b',1,2.88,7,'x']

my_other_list[-3:]
Out[28]:
[2.88, 7, 'x']
9

Given the following List:

my_list = [2,5,8,7,1,2,7]

How do you access the 3rd item in the list (i.e. 8)?

a) my_list[3]

b) my_list[2]

c) my_list[5]

d) my_list[7]

10

Given the following List:

my_list = [2,5,8,7,1,2,7]

How do you access the last 4 items in the list (i.e. 7,1,2,7)?

a) my_list[4]

b) my_list[-4:]

c) my_list[1:4]

d) my_list[2:4]

Dictionaries¶

Dictionaries are similar to "structure-arrays" in Matlab. A "Dictionary" stores items in a way that resembles a dictionary. You look up a "keyword" (e.g. "apple") and your immediately get the contents (i.e. "Red round fruit that tastes good").

Dictionaries are great to quickly find a specific item within the dictionary.

Lets make a dictionary:

In [29]:
my_dict = {'name':'Juan', 'age':27, 'gender':'male'}

my_dict
Out[29]:
{'name': 'Juan', 'age': 27, 'gender': 'male'}

To see if a variable is a Dictionary, you can also use type. See below:

In [30]:
type(my_dict)
Out[30]:
dict

Let's query the dictionary using the keywords:

In [31]:
my_dict['age']
Out[31]:
27
In [32]:
my_dict['name']
Out[32]:
'Juan'
11

Given the following Dictionary:

How do you access the contents stored under the 'age' key (i.e. 27)?

a) my_dict['name']

b) my_dict['age']

c) my_dict['gender']

d) None of the above

Functions and methods¶

Functions and methods are how you "do stuff" in Python. With one line of code you can do things like calculate a mean, or do a plot, or do a complicated statistical analysis. In essence, both functions and methods are code that accept an "input", do something to the input, and spits out an "output". The only thing you need to know and remember is the name of the function (or method). Arguably, learning Python is mostly learning the names of the available functions and methods.

Functions¶

Functions are used following the "nomenclature" below:

output = FunctionName(input)

We already used a few functions above, namely the "print" function...

In [33]:
print('hello world!')

hello world!

...and the "type" function

In [34]:
type(124.87)
Out[34]:
float

In both case the output was simply displayed to screen, which happens when you do not specify what to do with the output. Below are a few examples where the output is saved to a variable:

First lets do a list... and then apply some functions to it.

In [35]:

Methods¶

Methods are similar to functions, but they follow a different "nomenclature":

output = input.MethodName(arguments)

The arguments are additional information sometimes required by the method.

Note that before you can "apply" MethodName to the input object, we first need to create the input object.

For example...

In [40]:
# First we create a "list" object
mylist = [4,7,2,9,6,3,3,8,5,10]

# Then, this appends the number "2" to the end of mylist
mylist.append(2)

print(mylist)

[4, 7, 2, 9, 6, 3, 3, 8, 5, 10, 2]

Here the number 2 in the parenthesis is an argument.

Let do some more...

In [41]:
# This finds the number "7" in mylist, and removes it
mylist.remove(7)

print(mylist)

[4, 2, 9, 6, 3, 3, 8, 5, 10, 2]
In [42]:
#This sorts mylist. Note that this method does not require any arguments, thus the parenthesis are left empty ()
mylist.sort()

print(mylist)

[2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10]
In [43]:
#This finds the number "8" in mylist and returns its index
mylist.index(8)
Out[43]:
7

By now you probably figured out that each object type (e.g. lists or dictionaries) has its own built-in methods. Use Google to find out the available methods for a particular object type. For example, if you want to see the available methods for "list" objects, Google: python methods list

19

Given the following statement:

c = mylist.remove(7)

What is the "input"?

a) c

b) mylist

c) remove

d) 7

Given the following statement:

c = mylist.remove(7)

What is the "output"?

a) c

b) mylist

c) remove

d) 7

Given the following statement:

c = mylist.remove(7)

What is the "MethodName"?

a) c

b) mylist

c) remove

d) 7

22

Given the following statement:

c = mylist.remove(7)

What is the "argument"?

a) c

b) mylist

c) remove

d) 7

Modules¶

So far we used some of the built-in functions of Python (e.g. type, len, max), as well as some methods of Python's built-in objects (e.g. methods of the list object); however, there are A LOT MORE!. You can import functions and objects (with its associated methods) from external "modules" (or "packages")... therefore you have thousands of functions and methods at your disposal.

To be able to use a "module", you first need to (1) install the module, and then you need to (2) import the module.

  1. When you "install" a module, behind the scenes the module's code is downloaded from the cloud and written in the default "Python Directory" in your hard-drive. This step only needs to be done once. The module will remained installed in your hard-drive "forever" (or until you decide to uninstall it).

  2. When you "import" a module, behind the scenes the module's code is loaded into Memory (from the default "Python Directory" where it was installed in step 1). This step needs to be done every time you run the program that needs the module. Conveniently, you can simply use an import statement at the beginning of your code so the required module is loaded automatically every time you run your code.

When you install Anaconda, the Anaconda installer "installs" Python and also "installs" a bunch of commonly used modules. Therefore you can simply import them and use them right away. Below is an example about how to import the Module math and use one of its functions (note that we'll learn how to "install" new modules at the end of this lab).

In [44]:
# First import the module "math"
import math

# Then use the function "sin" within the module "math"
math.sin(mylist[0])
Out[44]:
0.9092974268256817

When using a function from an imported module, you need to add the module name to the function name. Thus the "nomenclature" is slightly modified as shown below:

output = ModuleName.FunctionName(input)

Installing new modules¶

Before we do our last "Real-life case study", we need to install 3 modules that do not come pre-installed with Anaconda. There are several ways to install Python modules and libraries, here we will use conda. Note that normally you only need to install a module once (it will remain installed until you manually remove it).

Most likely you already did this BEFORE the workshop started (instructions at the top of this manual). However, if you didn't here are the instructions to install the 3 modules (i.e. netcdf4, cartopy and cmocean). I'll explain what these modules do later.

When you need to install additional Python modules or libraries, you will need the Anaconda Prompt if you are in Windows, or if you are a Mac user, you can simply use Mac's built it terminal.

In Windows, search in the taskbar for "Anaconda Prompt" (in Mac, search for "terminal" in the Launchpad). The terminal should look a bit like this:

In the following case studies we will need the modules netcdf4, catopy and cmocean. You probably installed this BEFORE the beginning of this workshop. However, if you haven't installed them yet.... take a look at the instructions at the top of this document.

Real-life case study #1: data from an oceanographic buoy outside Halifax Harbour¶

Up to here, everything probably sounds easy, but not really that useful. Lets put it all together in a real-life application using 1 function and 1 method.

There is a weather/oceanic buoy that broadcast real-time data via the following server: https://www.smartatlantic.ca/erddap/tabledap/SMA_halifax.html


Smartatlantic buoy
Buoy location (Halifax, Canada)

The following code load the buoy's data, and makes a simple plot.

In Spyder's Editor open a new file and save it as buoy.py. Copy-paste the code below to your new file and click

In [62]:
# Import Pandas module
import pandas as pd

# Read data from file
buoy_data = pd.read_csv('./data/buoy_data.csv', skiprows=[1])

# Do quick plot
buoy_data.plot(x='time',y='surface_temp_avg', rot=90)
Out[62]:
<Axes: xlabel='time'>

To see the plot you just made, click on the "Plot" tab (beside your "Variable explorer"). See below...

Code Explanation:¶

Line 1:¶

In [61]:
import pandas as pd

Here we imported the pandas module, which is a fantastic data analysis library (learn more: http://pandas.pydata.org/ ). Note that we also "nicknamed" the module pd so that we don't have to write the long name "pandas" before each function.

Line 2:¶

In [63]:
buoy_data = pd.read_csv('./data/buoy_data.csv', skiprows=[1])

This line load the data from the file buoy_data.csv and puts it into a new variable that we called buoy_data. We named our variable with the same name as the file (i.e. buoy_data), but you can use any name you want (e.g. my_ocean_data). However, using variable names that describe "what's in them" is encouraged.

Below is the breakdown of the statement:

  • MethodName.FunctionName: pd.read_csv
  • Input: buoy_data.csv
  • output: buoy_data

So, we used 1 arguments in this example (i.e. buoy_data.csv), but how do we know what arguments are available and how to use them?

ANSWER: Google the function name (i.e. Google: pd.read_csv)

The output, buoy_data, is a pandas DataFrame object. We'll talk more about this below.

Note: you can also open the dataset directly from the server, as long as you know the url. In this case the commands would be:

In [13]:
url = "https://www.smartatlantic.ca/erddap/tabledap/SMA_halifax.csv?time%2Csurface_temp_avg&time%3E=2025-05-19T00%3A00%3A00Z&time%3C=2025-11-26T04%3A23%3A01Z"
buoy_data = pd.read_csv(url, skiprows=[1])

Line 3:¶

In [ ]:
buoy_data.plot(x='time',y='surface_temp_avg', rot=90)

Here we applied the method plot to the pandas DataFrame object buoy_data. The output is a plot!

Real-life case study #2: Plot real-time data from a Glider (Autonomous Underwater Vehicle)¶


Slocum Glider
2013 glider deployment in Roseway basin

The code below uses data from a glider that was deployed off the southern coast of Nova Scotia in 2013 (https://ceotr.ocean.dal.ca/gliders). The code makes a rough depth-vs-latitude scatter plot.

Plot temperature along latitude¶

In [4]:
# Make time object (datetime) from time string
glider_data['time (UTC)'] = pd.to_datetime(glider_data['time (UTC)'], format='%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')

# Plot temperature along latitude
glider_data.plot.scatter('latitude (degrees_north)',
                         'pressure (dbar)',
                         s = 30,
                         c='temperature (degree_C)',
                         marker='o',
                         edgecolor='none',
                         cmap='viridis',
                         ylim=[glider_data['pressure (dbar)'].max(),0],
                         figsize=[18,6])
Out[4]:
<Axes: xlabel='latitude (degrees_north)', ylabel='pressure (dbar)'>

The left side of the graph shows the data collected at the beginning of the deployment. The right side of the graph shows the most recently collected data. The top of the graph shows the temperature close to the surface (3 m) while data points at the bottom of the graph represent temperature near the bottom (~150 m). Note that there was a thermocline at about 20 m depth, where water temperature was noticeably warmer between 3 and 20 m.

Plot the glider's track¶


It is also useful to plot the glider path from above (i.e. "bird's eye" view). We can do that with the .plot method:
In [116]:
# Bird's eye view transect
glider_data.plot(x='longitude (degrees_east)',y='latitude (degrees_north)',style='.-', rot=90)
Out[116]:
<Axes: xlabel='longitude (degrees_east)'>

You can see that the glider went south-east and then came back north-west along the same path.

Real-life case study #3: Sea Surface Temperature from Satellites¶

Some satellites can measure Sea Surface Temperature (SST) using optical sensors that capture infrared radiation coming from the ocean.

If you haven't installed netcdf4, cartopy and cmocean yet.... take a look at the section at the top of this document. xarray should be already installed but if it is missing install in the same way.

For the following sections, we use "NetCDF" files, this is a binary format very compressed, made to store and transfer large datasets, but you cannot just open it in Excel. That is why we installed the netcdf4 and xarray modules. In the examples below we will use xarray to read netcdf files but you can also use netcdf4, as you prefer. An example of using netcdf4 you can look at the scripts sst.py and sst_composite.py in ./scripts/ and run them in Spyder or in the python terminal.

Note that the code below is pretty much "the real deal". It is as complicated as it gets with Python, yet it is just a series of statements declaring variables and applying functions and methods. By convention, at the top of the file you import all the modules you need.

Get data with ERDDAP¶

The data were already downloaded so you don't need to run the code below, but if you want to change the parameters feel free to edit lat/lon/time and run the cell to update the file.

Since we are interested in an area near the prime meridan, we need to download all longitudes, convert longitude from 0:360 to -180:180 and select the area of interest to limit file size.

In [16]:
import urllib.request 

lat = [-5,25]
lon = [0,360] # Longitude goes from 0 to 360 so we need to download all longitudes to plot accross prime meridian
time = '2025-11-10T12:00:00Z'

url = f"https://oceanwatch.pifsc.noaa.gov/erddap/griddap/CRW_sst_v3_1.nc?analysed_sst%5B({time}):1:({time})%5D%5B({lat[0]}):1:({lat[1]})%5D%5B({lon[0]}):1:({lon[1]})%5D" 

urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, "./data/sst.nc")

lon = [-35,15]
sst = xr.open_dataset("./data/sst.nc")
sst["longitude"] = (sst["longitude"] + 180) % 360 - 180
sst = sst.sortby("longitude");
sst = sst.sel(longitude=slice(lon[0],lon[1]))
sst.to_netcdf("./data/sst.nc")
del sst;

Load the data with xarray¶

In [3]:
import xarray as xr 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Load dataset
ds = xr.open_dataset('./data/sst.nc',decode_cf=True)

The code above loaded the .nc file. Now you have to dig in the file and see information about the variables that are included in the file. The information you need is (1) variable names, and (2) their dimenssions. To figure that out you can use the display function. Look inside the dataset with the display function. You can see that there is only 1 time entry.

As you can see, the variables (and thier shapes) in the .nc file are:

'time', shape = (1,)
'latitude', shape = (501,)
'longitude', shape = (1000,)
and 'analysed_sst', shape = (1, 501, 1000)

Make a rough plot with xarray¶

In [38]:
# Check this documentation for plotting with Xarray
# https://docs.xarray.dev/en/stable/user-guide/plotting.html

ds.analysed_sst.plot()
ax = plt.gca()
ax.set_xlim([-30,13])
ax.set_ylim([-5,25]);

Take a look at the generated map. You can see the colder water at the north, and warmer water in the center of the map.

What do you think is the average temperature in the whole map?

Luckily this is easy to find by applying the .mean method to out Sea Surface Temperature data (analysed_sst):
Note that you can add .values at the end of the command to get an unformatted output.

In [59]:
ds.analysed_sst.mean()
Out[59]:
array(27.2648722)

Lets see if you can figure out what are the minimum and the maximum temperatures is sst.

34

What is the minimum recorded Sea Surface Temperature in the sst data?

35

What is the maximum recorded Sea Surface Temperature in the sst data?

36

From the code above... which of the following are "functions" or "methods"?

Note that these "functions" or "methods" have fixed names, the coder has no choice but to use the correct "function" or "method" names.

Nicer maps (cartopy)¶

Lets do a slightly fancier map of the same data. This time using a "Mercator Projection".

Since the satellite data is still "in memory" (assuming that you executed the code above, and did not turn off your computer since then), we can simply create the new map with the new projection.

In this map we added some extra labels, colorbar and land mask, rivers.

In [49]:
import cartopy.crs as ccrs
import cartopy
import cartopy.feature as cfeature
import matplotlib.colors  as colors
import matplotlib.ticker as mticker
from cartopy.mpl.gridliner import LONGITUDE_FORMATTER, LATITUDE_FORMATTER

pc = ccrs.PlateCarree()
extent = [-30, 13, -5, 23] # lon_min/lon_max/lat_min/lat_max
cmin = 15
cmax = 30

norm1 = colors.Normalize(vmin=cmin, vmax=cmax)
rivers_50m = cfeature.NaturalEarthFeature('physical', 'rivers_lake_centerlines', '50m')

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))
ax1 = plt.axes(projection=ccrs.Mercator())

h1 = ds.analysed_sst.plot(ax=ax1, norm=norm1, add_colorbar=False, transform=pc)

# We choose a station to plot on the map, we will use this station to plot a time series below.
lat = 10
lon = 340

plt.plot(lon,lat,'r',marker='o', transform=pc)

ax1.set_extent(extent)
ax1.add_feature(cartopy.feature.LAND, edgecolor='none', facecolor='lightgrey', lw=0.5)
ax1.add_feature(cartopy.feature.LAKES, edgecolor='black', lw=0.5)
ax1.add_feature(rivers_50m, facecolor='None', edgecolor='black', lw=0.5)
ax1.coastlines(resolution='10m', color='k', linestyle='-', alpha=1, lw=0.5)

cxy = [0.50, 0.80, 0.40, 0.05]
cax = ax1.inset_axes(cxy)
cb = plt.colorbar(h1, ax=ax1, extend = 'neither', cax = cax, norm=norm1, orientation='horizontal')
cb.set_label('Sea Surface Temperature (˚C)')
cax.xaxis.set_ticks_position('top')
cax.xaxis.set_label_position('top')

gl = ax1.gridlines(crs=pc, draw_labels=True)
gl.xlabels_top = False
gl.ylabels_right = False
gl.xlines = False
gl.ylines = False
gl.xlocator = mticker.FixedLocator([-20, -10, 0, 10, 20])
gl.xformatter = LONGITUDE_FORMATTER
gl.yformatter = LATITUDE_FORMATTER

Cartopy is a powerful module to create maps. We don't have time to deep-dive into it today, but feel free to explore other projections and make some extra maps. Here are some Galleries:

https://cartopy.readthedocs.io/stable/gallery/index.html

Getting Satellite data at a specific location¶

Now we repeat the step from above but getting data only at a specific latitude/longitude (red dot in the figure above) and for a given time period.

The code below was previously run and the data saved in the data folder so you don't need to run it now, but you can play with it later.

In [50]:
import urllib.request 

lat = 10
lon = 340
tmin = '2020-11-12T12:00:00Z'
tmax = '2025-11-10T12:00:00Z'
url=f"https://oceanwatch.pifsc.noaa.gov/erddap/griddap/CRW_sst_v3_1.nc?analysed_sst%5B({tmin}):1:({tmax})%5D%5B({lat}):1:({lat})%5D%5B({lon}):1:({lon})%5D" 

urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, f"./data/sst_{lat}_{lon}.nc");

Open the saved dataset with xarray

In [51]:
import xarray as xr 

lat = 10
lon = 340

ds1 = xr.open_dataset(f"./data/sst_{lat}_{lon}.nc",decode_cf=True)

Look inside the file with display. You notice that now the dataset has only 1 longitude/latitude entry, but lots of time.

    summary :
    NOAA Coral Reef Watch Daily Global 5km Satellite Sea Surface Temperature (CoralTemp). CoralTemp is derived from three different but related 5km daily gap-free SST data sets and provides an internally consistent SST product that stretches from 1985 to present: Operational Sea Surface Temperature and Sea Ice Analysis (OSTIA) Sea Surface Temperature Reanalysis (1985-2002), Geo-Polar Blended Night-only Sea Surface Temperature Reanalysis (2002-2016), Geo-Polar Blended Night-only Sea Surface Temperature Near Real-Time (2017 to present).

We can make a quick plot with xarray

In [53]:
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(14,5))
ds1.analysed_sst.plot()
plt.xlabel('')
plt.ylabel('Sea surface temperature (˚C)')
plt.title(f'SST at {lat}˚N, {lon}˚W');

Real-life case study #4: ARGO floats¶


BGC Argo float
Map of active (green) and inactive (grey) BGC Argo floats with tracks

The code below uses data from an active BGC Argo float (#1902492) deployed off the Gulf of Guinea (https://maps.biogeochemical-argo.com/bgcargo/?&txt=1902492).

Argo floats are ocean profilers that drift with currents and periodically rise to the surface to record water column properties (temperature, salinity) and transmit the data via satellite (see schematic here). BGC Argo floats also measure biogeochemical variables such as oxygen, nitrate, pH, chlorophyll and light.

The float data were downloaded from https://tds0.ifremer.fr/thredds/fileServer/CORIOLIS-ARGO-GDAC-OBS/aoml/1902492/1902492_Sprof.nc and saved in the data folder

Load the data file and display the content¶

In [1]:
import xarray as xr

ds = xr.open_dataset('./data/1902492_Sprof.nc', decode_times=True)

display(ds)

Plot track of float (colored by time)¶

In [ ]:
import cartopy.crs as ccrs
import cartopy
import cartopy.feature as cfeature
import matplotlib.colors  as colors
import matplotlib.ticker as mticker
from cartopy.mpl.gridliner import LONGITUDE_FORMATTER, LATITUDE_FORMATTER
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
import matplotlib.pyplot  as plt
import cmocean

cm = cmocean.cm.thermal

pc = ccrs.PlateCarree()
extent = [-15, 13, -8, 15]

rivers_50m = cfeature.NaturalEarthFeature('physical', 'rivers_lake_centerlines', '50m')

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))
ax1 = plt.axes(projection=ccrs.Mercator())

plt.plot(ds.LONGITUDE,ds.LATITUDE,'-',color='gray',zorder=0, transform=pc)
h1 = plt.scatter(ds.LONGITUDE,ds.LATITUDE,c=mdates.date2num(ds.JULD), cmap=cm, s=50, edgecolors='black',zorder=1, transform=pc)

ax1.coastlines(resolution='10m', color='k', linestyle='-', alpha=1, lw=0.5)

ax1.set_extent(extent)
ax1.add_feature(cartopy.feature.LAND, edgecolor='none', facecolor='lightgrey', lw=0.5)
ax1.add_feature(cartopy.feature.LAKES, edgecolor='black', lw=0.5)
ax1.add_feature(rivers_50m, facecolor='None', edgecolor='black', lw=0.5)
ax1.coastlines(resolution='10m', color='k', linestyle='-', alpha=1, lw=0.5)

cxy = [0.0, 1.10, 1.0, 0.05]
cax = ax1.inset_axes(cxy)
cb = plt.colorbar(h1, ax=ax1, extend = 'neither', cax = cax, orientation='horizontal')
cax.xaxis.set_ticks_position('top')
cax.xaxis.set_label_position('top')

loc = mdates.AutoDateLocator()
cb.ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(loc)
cb.ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.ConciseDateFormatter(loc))


gl = ax1.gridlines(crs=pc, draw_labels=True)
gl.xlabels_top = False
gl.ylabels_right = False
gl.xlines = False
gl.ylines = False
gl.xlocator = mticker.FixedLocator([-20, -10, 0, 10, 20])
gl.xformatter = LONGITUDE_FORMATTER
gl.yformatter = LATITUDE_FORMATTER

import cmocean
import matplotlib.pyplot  as plt
import numpy as np

var = 'TEMP' # Try changing to TEMP, DOXY or NITRATE

if var == 'TEMP':
    vlabel = 'Temperature (˚C)'
    cm = cmocean.cm.thermal
elif var == 'DOXY':
    vlabel = 'Oxygen (micromole/kg)'
    cm = cmocean.cm.haline
elif var == 'NITRATE':
    vlabel = 'Nitrate (micromole/kg)'
    cm = cmocean.cm.deep_r

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(15,5))
ax = plt.gca()
plt.scatter(np.transpose(np.tile(ds.JULD.T, (521, 1)), (1, 0)),-ds.PRES,30,ds[var], cmap = cm)#,vmin=10,vmax=30)
ax.set_ylabel('Depth (m)')
ax.set_ylim([-750,0])
plt.colorbar(label=vlabel)

ax.autoscale(enable=True, axis='x', tight=True)

Try changing the variable in the line var = 'TEMP' to DOXY or NITRATE. This will plot the oxygen or nitrate profiles

Data Management with ERDDAP¶

">

Data management (as an administrator) is a complicated topic that requires months of training to do properly. But in summary, if you have oceanographic data that you need to store, manage, and serve to end-users... you should look into ERDDAP!

ERDDAP:

  • It was developed by NOAA as a free open-source software.
  • Allows computer-human downloads (i.e. through a browser).
  • Allows computer-computer downloads (i.e. no browser. E.g. download data using Python, R, Matlab, etc.).
  • Many Governments and Oceanographic Institutions now serve their data using ERDDAP.

Setting up an ERDDAP server (the administrator's job) is beyond the scope of this workshop. However, learning how to use it (as a client, or end-user) is easy, and incredibly useful.

Here is a list of a few ERDDAP servers:

  • NOAA CoastWatch: https://coastwatch.noaa.gov/erddap/index.html
  • Dalhousie University CEOTR: https://ceotr.ocean.dal.ca/erddap/index.html
  • Biological & Chemical Oceanography Data Management Office: https://erddap.bco-dmo.org/erddap/index.html
  • University of Hawaii: https://erddap.bco-dmo.org/erddap/index.html
  • PermafrontNet: https://data.permafrostnet.ca/erddap/index.html
  • University of British Columbia: https://salishsea.eos.ubc.ca/erddap/index.html
  • Ocean Networks Canada: https://dap.oceannetworks.ca/erddap/index.html
  • Smartatlantic: https://www.smartatlantic.ca/erddap/index.html

See a more complete list at https://erddap.github.io/

You can also use the following ERDDAP search engine to find ERRAP servers around the world: http://erddap.com/

Example of using an ERDDAP server¶

Go to https://coastwatch.noaa.gov/erddap/index.html

On the search box (top-right), search for: SST

You should see a list of data products. Find the product named "Sea Surface Temperature, NOAA Coral Reef Watch Daily Global 5km Satellite SST (CoralTemp), 1985-present, Daily".

Click on the "graph" link for that product (see arrow in image below)

You should be able to see a webpage similar to the one below:

From here, you should be able to click on the map (to center) and zoom in or out to get the region that you are interested in.

Then, on the field Then set the File Type: select .nc

Then, click on Download the Data or an Image

This should trigger a download of the data into your "Downloads" folder. Move this newly downloaded file to your "WYTEC2_Python_Workshop/data" folder.

In my case the downloaded file was named noaacrwsstDaily_2830_f4c9_5547_U1710527396048.nc, but for you it will be a different name.

Note that this data (i.e. "Sea Surface Temperature, NOAA Coral Reef Watch Daily Global 5km Satellite SST" aka: CoralTemp) is similar to the previous example that we just did before. But this data set does not have any gaps, because it is a composite of several gap-free data products.

Try exploring other data products from ERDDAP. As long as you choose "MAPS" (i.e. 2-dimensional geospatial products), you should be able to adapt the code above. Just pay attention to the name of the variables and their shapes. )
